newsitem.title: USA: Eight years after Valdez spill, recovery uneven.
newsitem.headline: Eight years after Valdez spill, recovery uneven.

text.p: Eight years after the Exxon Valdez oil spill, ecological recovery in Alaska's Prince William Sound has been sporadic and uneven but shown progress, scientists at a three-day conference said.

Only one species, the bald eagle, is considered fully recovered from the 1989 disaster, said scientists at the Exxon Valdez Oil Spill Trustee Council annual restoration workshop, which concluded Saturday.

Factors hampering recovery of other species in the icy sound and surrounding areas of Gulf of Alaska may be unrelated to the 11 million gallon spill, the nation's worst, said Bob Spies, chief scientist for the trustee council.
"These ecosystems are always in flux. They're always in a different state and once in a while, they undergo a great change," Spies said in a presentation Saturday.

The past eight years have brought changes and some ailments to marine and coastal species, from zooplankton and eelgrass to sea otters and killer whales, said said Ted Cooney, a University of Alaska Fairbanks marine scientist who has studied ocean current cycles.
But pinpointing the cause of the problems this long after the tanker disaster is difficult, he said.
"Nobody can be definitive and say, 'It was all spill effect,' or, 'It was all environmental effect,'" he said.

The trustee council, comprising three state and three federal representatives, is responsibile for administering the $900 million that Exxon pledged to pay over 10 years to settle goverment civil damage claims arising from the spill.

The final payment is due in 2001. By then, the council estimates it will have spent $288 million on research and restoration and $386 million on acquiring land parcels to protect them from logging and other environment-degrading development.
The remainder of the settlement money was expected to go to continued cleanup programs, reimbursement for past cleanup costs, public education and administration.
